title: A Autopsy for the Ledger
premise: Gideon Fairweather, the coroner of the fading mill town of Harrow's Bend, is handed a missing-persons case file that should have been closed years ago: Lena Voss, drowned in the reservoir. But when her recovered diary keeps writing entries after her disappearance — in handwriting Gideon slowly realizes matches their own late mother's — they discover Lena faked her death to escape the town's founding family, who have been quietly erasing inconvenient people for three generations. The 'dead witness' everyone swears against is Lena herself, hiding in plain sight as the hospice nurse tending Gideon's dying aunt. To save her from a second, permanent death, Gideon must burn the ledger of names that bought their own family's survival, ending with Gideon testifying at a hearing that finally gives the erased their graves back.
about_author: Rafael Okonkwo spent a decade as a records clerk in county courthouses before turning to fiction, and his mysteries are known for their obsession with paper trails and the dead who leave none. He lives in a converted funeral parlor on the coast of Maine, where he claims the filing cabinets still whisper.

chapters.title: The Date That Wouldn't Die
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Sorting the estate sale boxes of the long-dead Voss house, Gideon finds Lena's diary and notices entries continuing eleven days past her disappearance. The final entry names someone: 'He knows I know about the ledger.' The beat is quiet dread — the professional calm of a coroner cracking for the first time in years.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Walking the cemetery to ground themselves, Gideon catalogs the Voss-era deaths: four drownings, all ruled accidental, all within one decade. Sheriff Dane Pruitt dismisses the diary as grief-fueled forgery. The emotional beat is isolation — Gideon realizing the whole town would rather the dead stay tidy.

chapters.title: What the Water Kept
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, with an intercut of Lena's diary entries in italics. Exhumation of Lena's casket reveals it full of river stones — she was never buried. The diary entries reveal her terror of the Aldermere family, whose mill employs half the town. The beat is vertigo: the case isn't cold, it's alive.

chapters.title: The Nurse Who Knew Too Much
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. At Aunt Cora's bedside, Gideon notices the hospice nurse, 'Marisol,' hums a song that appears in the diary's margins — Lena's lullaby. Marisol deflects with practiced warmth, but her hands shake. The beat is electric suspicion wrapped in tenderness; Gideon can't decide if they've found a ghost or a target.

chapters.title: Inheritance of Debts
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Digging into their mother's effects, Gideon finds the Fairweather name in the Aldermere ledger — a payment made the year their mother changed her surname and fled here. The price of survival was silence. The beat is betrayal turned inward: Gideon has been hunting a conspiracy their own blood helped bury.

chapters.title: Nine Names
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The ledger lists nine erased townspeople across sixty years, each marked 'resolved' in the same clerk's hand. When Gideon photographs the pages, someone ransacks their office that night and takes the original — but not the copy hidden in a coffin they'd prepared for themselves. The beat is fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Dead Witness, Living Room
chapters.summary: Lena's POV (first time). Lena/Marisol watches Gideon sleep off a drugged tea she didn't order, realizing the Aldermeres are closing in on both of them. She decides to trust the coroner who dug up her stones. The beat is desperate hope — two people deciding to stop surviving alone.

chapters.title: Confession at the Reservoir
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the dam where Lena 'drowned,' she tells Gideon everything: the night she ran, the clerk who helped her, the price Cora paid to warn her. They're spotted by Dane Pruitt — who lowers his flashlight and says he's been waiting twenty years for someone else to see it too. The beat is alliance, fragile and hard-won.

chapters.title: The Burning Hour
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The Aldermere heir, Whit, corners them at the crematory to reclaim the ledger by fire — and Cora, lucid for the first time in months, walks in between them and names him as the man who killed her brother. In the struggle the ledger burns anyway, but Gideon photographed every page. The beat is climax: fury, sacrifice, and the truth finally spoken aloud.

chapters.title: A Grave for Everyone
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, epilogue six months later. The state hearings end; nine headstones are cut, including one for Lena Voss — left deliberately blank above ground while she, as Marisol, sits beside Gideon at Cora's hospice window. Gideon closes the last unsolved file and writes a new first entry in a fresh ledger: names of the living. The beat is earned peace — identity chosen, inheritance refused, survival finally unpaid.
